decks.title: Grammar for the Board — Part 1: Determiners, Tenses and Modals
goals: Choose articles, demonstratives and quantifiers correctly in context
Use time clues to select the right tense in gap-filling and editing tasks
Pick the modal that matches the meaning: ability, permission, obligation, advice or possibility
Apply a four-step routine to any one-mark grammar item

slides.heading: Grammar for the Board — Part 1: Determiners, Tenses and Modals
slides.body_md: CBSE Class 10 English, **Section B**. In the board paper the grammar question has **12 short tasks; you answer any 10** (1 mark each). This part covers determiners, tenses and modals. Part 2 covers concord, reported speech, editing and omission.

rows: Write or choose the missing word
Find the wrong or missing word and correct it
Rewrite a sentence in another form

visual.alt: Table of the three kinds of board grammar tasks: gap filling tests determiners, tenses, modals and concord; editing and omission test concord, tense, articles and prepositions; transformation tests reported speech.
visual.caption: Board pattern: 12 one-mark tasks, attempt any 10 (CBSE 2026-27, Section B).

slides.narration: Welcome! Grammar is the most dependable ten marks in your English paper. In the board exam, one question gives you twelve short tasks and you choose any ten, one mark each. The tasks are gap filling, editing and transformation. In this first part we master three tools: determiners, tenses and modals. Each one is about reading clues in the sentence, not memorising rules in isolation.

slides.heading: A four-move routine for every grammar item
slides.body_md: Most mistakes come from looking only at the blank. The answer is hidden in the words **around** it.

nodes.label: Find the clue: subject, time word, meaning, next noun
Re-read the sentence in your head

visual.alt: Flow of four steps: read the whole sentence, find the clue, choose and write the answer, then re-read the sentence.
visual.caption: Use this routine on every item.

slides.narration: Here is a routine you can use for every item. First, read the whole sentence, not just the blank. Second, hunt for the clue: who is the subject, what is the time word, what does the speaker mean, and which noun comes next. Third, choose and write your answer neatly. Fourth, read the sentence again in your head. If it sounds odd, go back to the clue.

slides.heading: Determiners: small words that point to a noun
slides.body_md: A determiner comes **before** a noun (and before any adjective) and tells us *which one*, *whose*, or *how much / how many*: *these ripe mangoes*, never *ripe these mangoes*.

rows: *The* bus to Andheri is late again.
my, your, his, her, its, our, their
some, any, much, many, few, little, each, every, enough
*Every* seat in the hall was taken.

visual.alt: Table of five kinds of determiners with examples: articles, demonstratives, possessives, quantifiers and numbers, each used in an example sentence.

slides.narration: A determiner is a small word that stands before a noun and tells us which one, whose, or how much. Articles, demonstratives like this and those, possessives like my and their, quantifiers like some and every, and numbers are all determiners. Notice that the determiner also comes before any adjective. We say these ripe mangoes, never ripe these mangoes.

slides.heading: A, an or the?
columns:
**a / an — any one, or first mention.** Choose by the first **sound**, not the letter:

- *an* hour, *an* honest man, *an* MLA
- *a* uniform, *a* one-rupee coin, *a* European city

**the — a particular one the listener knows:**

- already mentioned: *I bought a pen. The pen leaks.*
- only one exists: *the* Sun, *the* Internet
- superlatives: *the* tallest girl in class
- rivers, seas, mountain ranges: *the* Ganga, *the* Himalayas
slides.narration: Use a or an when you mean any one thing, or mention it for the first time. The choice depends on the sound, not the spelling. An hour, because the h is silent. A uniform, because it starts with a you sound. Use the when the listener knows exactly which one: something already mentioned, something unique like the Sun, a superlative like the tallest, or the names of rivers and mountain ranges.

slides.heading: Quantifiers: can you count the noun?
slides.body_md: *A few / a little* = some (positive). *Few / little* = hardly any (negative). Uncountable nouns never take *a / an*: say *some advice*, not *an advice*.

visual.alt: Table of quantifiers: many, a few, few, a number of, each and every go with countable nouns; much, a little, little and an amount of go with uncountable nouns; some, any, enough, a lot of, no and most go with both.
visual.caption: A few / a little = positive; few / little = negative.

slides.narration: Before choosing a quantifier, ask one question: can I count this noun? Friends and books can be counted, so we say many and a few. Water, time and advice cannot, so we say much and a little. Some, any and enough work with both. And remember how one tiny article changes the meaning: a few friends is good news, but few friends is sad news.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: determiners in a notice
slides.body_md: Fill the blanks: *(1) ___ students of Class X must bring (2) ___ umbrella to the excursion. There is (3) ___ shade at the dam site, so (4) ___ water bottle is also required.*
bullets: (1) **All** — the notice addresses every student and *students* is plural (*each* would need a singular noun).
(2) **an** — *umbrella* begins with a vowel sound.
(3) **little** — the meaning is *hardly any*, and *shade* is uncountable.
(4) **a** — one bottle; *water* here describes the bottle, which begins with a consonant sound.
slides.narration: Let us solve a notice together. Blank one comes before students, a plural noun, and the notice speaks to everyone, so all fits, while each would need a singular noun. Blank two comes before umbrella, which starts with a vowel sound, so an. Blank three: the meaning is that there is hardly any shade, and shade cannot be counted, so little without a. Blank four: one bottle, so a.

slides.heading: Check: choose the quantifier
slides.narration: Your turn. Look at the noun after the blank. Can it be counted? Then read the end of the sentence. Does it suggest a small but sufficient amount, or almost nothing? Pick your answer, then read the explanation.

slides.heading: Tenses are a grid: time plus aspect
slides.body_md: Every tense = a **time** (present, past, future) + an **aspect** (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous). Learn one row and the others follow.

visual.alt: Grid of the twelve tense forms of the verb play: present, past and future across simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous.
visual.caption: Every tense = a time + an aspect.

slides.narration: English tenses look like twelve separate rules, but they are really a grid. Across the top is the aspect: simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous. Down the side is the time: present, past and future. Once you know the pattern for one row, the others follow. For example, has played, had played and will have played are all perfect forms, only at different times.

slides.heading: Time clues tell you the tense
slides.body_md: The board almost always plants a clue word. Underline it before you choose.

rows: already, just, yet, ever; since / for up to now
We *moved* to Pune two years ago.
by the time / before + another past action
The show *had started* by the time we arrived.
will / be going to / simple present for timetables

visual.alt: Table linking time clues to tenses: habits take the simple present, now takes the present continuous, already and since take the present perfect, yesterday and ago take the simple past, by the time takes the past perfect, and tomorrow takes future forms.

slides.narration: Look for the clue word. Every day signals a habit, so the simple present. Now, or look, signals the present continuous. Already, just, yet, since and for signal the present perfect. Yesterday, ago and last week signal the simple past, and they never go with has or have. By the time, together with another past action, signals the past perfect.

slides.heading: Two tense pairs that cost marks
columns:
**Present perfect vs simple past**

- *I have lost my ID card.* (still lost now)
- *I lost my ID card yesterday.* (finished time named)
- Wrong: *I have lost it yesterday.*

**Past perfect vs simple past**

- *When we reached the stadium, the match had begun.* (it began first)
- *When we reached the stadium, the match began.* (it began as we arrived)
slides.narration: Two pairs confuse students most. First, present perfect versus simple past. Use has or have when the result matters now and no finished time is given. The moment you name a finished time, like yesterday, switch to the simple past. Second, past perfect versus simple past. If one past action happened before another, the earlier one takes had. Changing the tense actually changes the story.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: tenses in a diary entry
slides.body_md: Fill the blanks: *I (1) ___ (wait) at the bus stop for forty minutes when it finally came. By then it (2) ___ (start) to drizzle. Since that evening I (3) ___ (carry) an umbrella every day.*
bullets: (1) **had been waiting** — an action lasting up to a past moment (*when it finally came*)
(2) **had started** — finished before the bus came (*By then*)
(3) **have been carrying** (also *have carried*) — *since* + continuing till today
slides.narration: Here the clues do all the work. For forty minutes, up to a moment in the past when the bus came, gives had been waiting. By then tells us the drizzle began before that moment, so had started. Since that evening, continuing until today, gives have been carrying, or have carried. Each answer comes straight from a clue word, not from guesswork.

slides.heading: Check: which action came first?
slides.narration: Try this one. There are two past actions in the sentence. Ask yourself which happened first, and which tense marks the earlier of two past actions.

slides.heading: Modals: the meaning decides
slides.body_md: A modal is followed by the **base verb** with no *to*: *must go*, not *must to go*. (Only *ought to* and *have to* take *to*.)

visual.alt: Table of modal meanings: ability, permission, obligation, no obligation, prohibition, advice and possibility, with the modals and an example for each.

slides.narration: Modals are helping verbs that add a meaning: ability, permission, obligation, advice or possibility. In gap filling, the meaning of the whole sentence tells you which modal fits. A law or rule means must. A suggestion means should. Something unnecessary means need not, and something forbidden means must not. And never put to after a modal. We say must go, not must to go.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: choose the modal by meaning
slides.body_md: Ask: *rule, advice, permission, ability, guess or request?* Then pick the modal.
bullets: *You ___ wear goggles in the chemistry lab; it is a safety rule.* → **must** (rule)
*You ___ bring chart paper; the school will provide it.* → **need not** (unnecessary)
*Ravi ___ be in the canteen; his bag is still here.* → **might / may / could** (a guess)
*___ you help me carry these registers, please?* → **Could / Can / Would** (polite request)
slides.narration: Watch how one question settles each blank: what is the speaker doing? In the first sentence a safety rule is stated, so must. In the second the school will provide the paper, so bringing it is not necessary: need not. In the third we are only guessing, so might, may or could. In the last, someone politely asks for help, so could you, or would you.

slides.heading: Check: not necessary or not allowed?
slides.narration: Check yourself. A holiday means you do not have to come. Is that a prohibition, or simply no need? Choose carefully, because the two options look alike.

slides.heading: Check: spot the polite request
slides.narration: One more. Four sentences use four different modals. Only one of them is a polite request. Which one would you say to a neighbour whose music is too loud?

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Read the whole sentence; the clue is **around** the blank.
Determiners: *a / an* by sound; *the* for a particular one; countable or uncountable decides the quantifier.
Tenses = time + aspect; *yesterday, ago, last week* never go with *has / have*.
Past perfect marks the **earlier** of two past actions.
Modals follow meaning; base verb after a modal; *need not* is not *must not*.

rows: since or for, continuing till now
the earlier of two past actions

visual.alt: Summary table: a vowel sound leads to an; an uncountable noun to much or a little; since or for to the present perfect; the earlier of two past actions to the past perfect; a rule to must; something unnecessary to need not.

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part One. Always read the whole sentence. For determiners, listen to the first sound and ask whether the noun can be counted. For tenses, find the time clue, and remember that finished times never take has or have. For modals, decide what the speaker is doing, and keep the verb after the modal in its base form.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how grammar marks are won and lost
bullets: Write the **item number and only the answer**, clearly: *(iv) had moved*. Do not copy the whole passage.
In editing, show the **incorrect word and its correction** side by side, exactly as the question asks.
Spelling counts: *received, necessary, occurred*. A misspelt answer can lose the mark.
Do the ten items you are surest of first, and follow the instruction on how many to attempt.
Classic traps: *has gone … yesterday*, *did not went*, *must to go*, *an university*, *few* for *a few*.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Write the item number and only the answer, clearly. In editing, show both the wrong word and its correction. Spell carefully, because a misspelt answer can lose the mark. Do the ten items you are surest of first, and follow the instruction on how many to attempt. Watch for five classic traps: has with yesterday, did with went, must with to, an before university, and few in place of a few.

decks.title: Grammar for the Board — Part 2: Concord, Reported Speech, Editing and Omission
goals: Make verbs agree with singular, plural, collective and compound subjects
Convert statements, questions, commands and requests into reported speech
Change pronouns, tenses and time words correctly when reporting
Detect and correct errors and omissions in a short passage

slides.heading: Grammar for the Board — Part 2: Concord, Reported Speech, Editing and Omission
slides.body_md: Part 2 of the Class 10 grammar lesson. **Editing** tasks test concord and tense in disguise, and **transformation** tasks are usually reported speech. Master these three skills and most of Section B grammar is covered.

rows: Write or choose the missing word
Find the wrong or missing word and correct it
Rewrite a sentence in another form

visual.alt: Table of the three kinds of board grammar tasks: gap filling tests determiners, tenses, modals and concord; editing and omission test concord, tense, articles and prepositions; transformation tests reported speech.
visual.caption: Board pattern: 12 one-mark tasks, attempt any 10 (CBSE 2026-27, Section B).

slides.narration: Welcome to Part Two. Here we cover three skills that the board loves to test. Subject verb concord, which hides inside most editing errors. Reported speech, which is the usual transformation task. And editing and omission, where you hunt for one wrong or missing word in each line. By the end you will have a method for each.

slides.heading: Concord: find the real subject first
slides.body_md: The verb agrees with its **subject**, not with the noun nearest to it. Cover up the *of*-phrase and see what is left.
bullets: *The box of sweets **is** on the table.* (subject: box)
*One of my cousins **lives** in Dubai.* (subject: one)
*The quality of the roads **has** improved.* (subject: quality)
slides.narration: Concord means the verb agrees with its subject. The trap is that the noun nearest to the verb is often not the subject. In the box of sweets is on the table, the subject is box, not sweets. A quick trick: cover the phrase beginning with of, and see what is left. One of my cousins lives in Dubai. Cover of my cousins, and you get one lives.

slides.heading: Nine concord rules in one table
slides.body_md: Most editing errors in board papers come from these rules.

rows: Rina and her brother *are* in Class X.
Bread and butter *is* enough for me.
A as well as / along with / with B
The captain, with his players, *is* here.
either A or B; neither A nor B
Neither Ravi nor his friends *were* invited.
a number of / the number of
A number of buses *are* late; the number of buses *is* small.
a sum of money, time or distance

visual.alt: Table of nine concord rules with examples, covering and, each and every, as well as, either or, collective nouns, a number of, amounts, and nouns like physics and news.

slides.narration: Here are the rules that cover almost every exam sentence. Two subjects joined by and are plural, unless they name one thing, like bread and butter. Each, every, either and neither are singular. With as well as or along with, look only at the first subject. With either or and neither nor, the nearer subject wins. Amounts, and nouns like physics and news, are singular.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: correcting concord errors
slides.body_md: Each sentence has one concord error. Find the subject, then fix the verb.
bullets: *The quality of the mangoes are excellent.* → subject *quality* → **is**
*Neither the principal nor the teachers was informed.* → nearer subject *teachers* → **were**
*Every boy and girl were given a sapling.* → *every* makes it singular → **was**
*The committee have announced its decision.* → one unit (*its*) → **has**
slides.narration: Let us correct four sentences. In the first, cover of the mangoes, and the subject is quality, so is. In the second, neither nor, so the nearer subject, teachers, decides: were. In the third, every in front of boy and girl makes the whole subject singular: was. In the fourth, the word its shows the committee acting as one unit, so has.

slides.heading: Check: neither … nor
slides.narration: Your turn. With neither and nor, which subject does the verb agree with? Find it, decide if it is singular or plural, and check the time of the sentence.

slides.heading: Reported speech: the tense steps back
slides.body_md: After a **past** reporting verb (*said, told, asked*), each tense moves one step into the past. Pronouns change to fit who is speaking to whom.

visual.alt: Table of tense backshift in reported speech: am, is, are become was or were; do becomes did; is doing becomes was doing; did and has done become had done; will, can, may become would, could, might; must stays or becomes had to.
visual.caption: No backshift if the reporting verb is present (says) or the statement is a universal truth.

slides.narration: When we report what someone said, using a past reporting verb like said or asked, the tense usually steps one place back into the past. Is becomes was, do becomes did, has done becomes had done, and will becomes would. There are two exceptions. If the reporting verb is in the present, like says, nothing changes. And universal truths stay in the present.

slides.heading: Time and place words shift too
slides.body_md: The report is made at another time and place, so *here* and *now* move with it.

rows: the previous day / the day before
the next day / the following day

visual.alt: Table of time and place word changes: now to then, today to that day, yesterday to the previous day, tomorrow to the next day, ago to before, last week to the previous week, this to that, here to there.

slides.narration: Time and place words also shift, because the report is made later and somewhere else. Now becomes then. Today becomes that day. Yesterday becomes the previous day, and tomorrow becomes the next day or the following day. This becomes that, and here becomes there. Learn this table as pairs, and practise saying them aloud.

slides.heading: Four sentence types, four patterns
slides.body_md: Decide the **type** first; the type gives you the reporting verb and the linking word.

rows: She said that she was ready.
He asked if I was ready.

visual.alt: Table of four sentence types in reported speech: statements use said or told with that; yes or no questions use asked with if or whether; wh-questions use asked with the wh-word; commands and requests use told or requested with a to-infinitive.

slides.narration: Every line of a dialogue is one of four types. A statement is reported with said or told, and that. A yes or no question uses asked, and if or whether. A wh question keeps its wh word, like where or why. A command or request uses told, ordered or requested, followed by to and the verb, or not to for a negative.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: reporting a dialogue, step by step
slides.body_md: Doctor: *"Have you been sleeping well?"* Rhea: *"No, I wake up at night because of my cough."*
bullets: Step 1, type: line 1 is a yes/no question; line 2 is a statement.
Step 2, verb and link: *asked … if*; *replied that*.
Step 3, pronouns: *you → she*; *I → she*, *my → her*.
Step 4, tenses: *have been sleeping → had been sleeping*; *wake → woke*.
Result: *The doctor asked Rhea if she had been sleeping well. Rhea replied that she had not, as she woke up at night because of her cough.*
slides.narration: Follow four steps. First, the type: the doctor asks a yes or no question, and Rhea makes a statement. Second, the reporting verb and link: asked if, and replied that. Third, the pronouns: you becomes she, and I and my become she and her. Fourth, the tenses step back: have been sleeping becomes had been sleeping, and wake becomes woke. Her no becomes she had not.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: the question-order trap
slides.body_md: The guard said to me, *"Where are you going with this parcel?"*
bullets: Wrong: *The guard asked me where was I going with that parcel.*
Right: *The guard asked me where **I was going** with that parcel.*
After the wh-word use **statement order** (subject + verb), drop the question mark, and change *this → that*.
slides.narration: This is the most common error in reported questions. In a direct question the verb comes before the subject: where are you going. In reported speech, the question has become part of a statement, so the order returns to normal: where I was going. Drop the question mark too, and remember that this parcel becomes that parcel.

slides.heading: Check: report the wh-question
slides.narration: Check yourself. Which option keeps the wh word, uses statement order, and steps the tense back? Watch out for options that still sound like questions.

slides.heading: Editing: the six usual suspects
slides.body_md: Editing errors are planted in a few families. Test each line against them in this order.

rows: He spoke confident. I will recieve it.

visual.alt: Table of six error families in editing tasks with a wrong and a corrected example: tense, concord, article, preposition, pronoun, and word form or spelling.

slides.narration: Editing errors are not random. Examiners plant them in six families: tense, concord, articles, prepositions, pronouns, and word forms or spellings. Read each line and test it against these families one by one. Is the tense right for the time clue? Does the verb agree with the subject? Is an article missing or wrong? Is there an extra preposition, as in reached to?

slides.heading: Omission: hearing the missing word
slides.body_md: The missing word is usually small: an **article**, a **preposition**, a **helping verb**, a **pronoun** or a **conjunction**. Write the word before, the missing word, and the word after.

nodes.label: Read the line in pairs of words
Ask: article? preposition? helper verb? pronoun?
Write word before + missing word + word after

visual.alt: Flow of four steps for omission: read in pairs of words, find where it jolts, ask which kind of word is missing, write the words before and after with the missing word.

slides.narration: In an omission task, one small word has been removed from a line. It is usually an article, a preposition, a helping verb, a pronoun or a conjunction. Read the line slowly in pairs of words and notice where it jolts. Then write three words: the word before the gap, the missing word, and the word after. That shows the examiner exactly where it goes.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: an editing passage
slides.body_md: *Each line has one error.* (1) My grandmother have a small kitchen garden. (2) She grow tomatoes, chillies and curry leaves. (3) Every mornings she waters the plants. (4) Last week she give a basket of tomatoes to our neighbours.

visual.alt: Table of answers to the editing example: have to has, grow to grows, mornings to morning, give to gave, with the reason for each.

slides.narration: Let us edit line by line. Line one: the subject is my grandmother, singular, so have becomes has. Line two: a habit, with she, so grow becomes grows. Line three: every needs a singular noun, so mornings becomes morning. Line four: last week is a finished time, so give becomes gave. Notice that three of the four errors are concord or tense.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: an omission passage
slides.body_md: *One word is missing in each line.* (1) Diwali is festival of lights. (2) We clean our house week before. (3) My mother draws rangoli the entrance.

visual.alt: Table of answers to the omission example: is a festival, house a week, rangoli at the entrance.

slides.narration: Now omissions. In line one, festival is a singular countable noun with no determiner, so is a festival. In line two, a week before, again an article. In line three, rangoli the entrance jolts, because a preposition of place is missing: rangoli at the entrance. Write each answer as before word, missing word, after word.

slides.heading: Check: correct the sentence
slides.narration: Try this editing item. The subject begins with neither of. Is neither singular or plural? Then choose the option that fixes only what is wrong.

slides.heading: Check: complete the reported statement
slides.narration: Last check. Two changes are needed in the reported statement: the tense of the verb, and the time word. Fill both blanks, then compare with the answer.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Concord: cover the *of*-phrase to find the real subject; *each / every / neither* are singular; with *either … or*, the nearer subject wins.
Reported speech: type → reporting verb and link → pronouns → tense backshift → time and place words.
Questions become statements: *asked where I was going*, never *where was I going*.
Editing: test tense, concord, article, preposition, pronoun, word form.
Omission: write the word before + missing word + word after.

nodes.label: Find the real subject → make the verb agree
Identify the sentence type → pick verb and link
Edit: test the six error families line by line

visual.alt: Flow summarising Part 2: find the real subject for concord, identify the sentence type in reported speech, change pronouns, tenses and time words, and test six error families when editing.

slides.narration: To sum up Part Two. For concord, find the real subject before you touch the verb. For reported speech, work in order: type, reporting verb and link, pronouns, tense, and time words, and turn questions into statements. For editing, test each line against the six error families. For omissions, write the word before, the missing word, and the word after.

slides.heading: Exam tips: editing and transformation
bullets: Use the format asked: *incorrect word → correction*, or *word before + missing word + word after*.
One error per line: do not "correct" a line that is already right in other places.
In reported speech, the tense, pronoun **and** time word must all be right for the mark.
Never put a question mark or *that* before a wh-word in a reported question.
Keep the meaning: *must not* is not *need not*; *requested* for *please*, *ordered* for commands.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Use exactly the format the question asks for. There is only one error in each line, so do not rewrite parts that are already correct. In reported speech, the mark usually needs the tense, the pronoun and the time word all to be right. Never add a question mark, or the word that, before a wh word. And keep the meaning: requested for please, and ordered for a command.

notes.title: Grammar — Class 10 board notes

sections.heading: 1. How the grammar question works
sections.body_md:
Section B of the CBSE Class 10 English paper has a grammar question of **12 one-mark tasks, of which you attempt any 10**. The tasks are **gap filling** (determiners, tenses, modals, concord), **editing** (spot the error, write the correction) and **transformation** (usually reported speech). Some items give options, others ask you to write the word.

**Routine for every item:** read the whole sentence → find the clue (subject, time word, meaning, the noun after the blank) → write the answer → re-read the sentence.

key_terms.definition_md: A word near the blank that decides the answer: a time expression (*since, yesterday*), the subject (*each of*), or the noun that follows (*advice, students*).

rows: Write or choose the missing word
Find the wrong or missing word and correct it
Rewrite a sentence in another form

visual.alt: Table of the three kinds of board grammar tasks: gap filling tests determiners, tenses, modals and concord; editing and omission test concord, tense, articles and prepositions; transformation tests reported speech.
visual.caption: Board pattern: 12 one-mark tasks, attempt any 10 (CBSE 2026-27, Section B).

sections.heading: 2. Determiners
sections.body_md:
A determiner comes before a noun and any adjective, and fixes *which one* or *how much / how many*.

- **a / an** by the first **sound**: *an hour, an MLA, a uniform, a one-way street*.
- **the** for a particular or unique thing, superlatives, rivers, seas and mountain ranges: *the Sun, the best answer, the Narmada*.
- No article before most proper names of people and cities, or before uncountable nouns used in general: *Advice is free.*
- **Countable vs uncountable:** *many / a few / few* + countable plural; *much / a little / little* + uncountable; *some / any / enough* + both.
- **Positive vs negative:** *a few, a little* = some; *few, little* = hardly any.
- **each / every / either / neither** + singular noun; **each of / neither of** + *the* + plural noun.

key_terms.definition_md: A noun with no plural, used with *much / a little*: advice, information, luggage, furniture, milk, homework.
A determiner of amount or number: some, any, many, much, few, little, each, every, enough.

visual.alt: Table of quantifiers: many, a few, few, a number of, each and every go with countable nouns; much, a little, little and an amount of go with uncountable nouns; some, any, enough, a lot of, no and most go with both.

sections.heading: 3. Tenses
sections.body_md:
Every tense = **time** (present, past, future) + **aspect** (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous). Choose by the clue word.

- **Simple present:** habits, facts, timetables — *The canteen opens at 8.*
- **Present continuous:** now, temporary — *She is staying with her aunt this month.*
- **Present perfect:** past action, present result, no finished time — *I have misplaced my calculator.*
- **Present perfect continuous:** *since / for* up to now — *We have been waiting since noon.*
- **Simple past:** finished time — *He topped the test last week.*
- **Past continuous:** in progress at a past moment — *I was revising when the lights went out.*
- **Past perfect:** the earlier of two past actions — *The bell had rung before I reached.*
- **Future:** *will* (decision, prediction), *be going to* (plan, evidence), simple present (timetable), and simple present after *if / when* — *If it rains, we will stay in.*

**State verbs** (know, like, own, believe, understand) are not normally used in continuous forms: *I know*, not *I am knowing*.

key_terms.definition_md: Moving a tense one step into the past, as in reported speech: is → was, has done → had done.
A verb describing a state, not an action (know, belong, prefer); rarely used in the -ing form.

rows: already, just, yet, ever; since / for up to now
We *moved* to Pune two years ago.
by the time / before + another past action
The show *had started* by the time we arrived.
will / be going to / simple present for timetables

visual.alt: Table linking time clues to tenses: habits take the simple present, now takes the present continuous, already and since take the present perfect, yesterday and ago take the simple past, by the time takes the past perfect, and tomorrow takes future forms.

sections.heading: 4. Modals
sections.body_md:
Modals add meaning to a main verb and are followed by the **base form without *to***: *can swim, must leave, should rest* (exceptions: *ought to, have to*).

- **can / could:** ability (*could* = past ability), informal permission, polite requests (*Could you…?*).
- **may / might:** formal permission (*May I…?*), possibility (*might* = less sure).
- **must / have to:** obligation; **must not:** prohibition.
- **need not / don't have to:** no obligation.
- **should / ought to:** advice, duty.
- **would:** polite requests (*Would you…?*), and the past of *will* in reported speech.

key_terms.definition_md: *Must not* = it is forbidden. *Need not* = it is not necessary (but allowed).

visual.alt: Table of modal meanings: ability, permission, obligation, no obligation, prohibition, advice and possibility, with the modals and an example for each.

sections.heading: 5. Subject–verb concord
sections.body_md:
The verb agrees with the **real subject**. Cover the *of*-phrase or the *along with*-phrase and look at what is left.

Key rules: *A and B* → plural (unless one idea: *rice and dal is*); *each, every, either, neither, everyone, nobody* → singular; *as well as / along with / with* → agree with the first subject; *either … or / neither … nor* → agree with the nearer subject; collective nouns acting as one unit → singular (*the team has*); *a number of* → plural, *the number of* → singular; amounts → singular (*Fifty rupees is enough*); *news, mathematics, physics* → singular.

key_terms.definition_md: A noun for a group treated as one unit: team, jury, committee, family, class. Usually singular in Indian and British exam English when the group acts together.

rows: Rina and her brother *are* in Class X.
Bread and butter *is* enough for me.
A as well as / along with / with B
The captain, with his players, *is* here.
either A or B; neither A nor B
Neither Ravi nor his friends *were* invited.
a number of / the number of
A number of buses *are* late; the number of buses *is* small.
a sum of money, time or distance

visual.alt: Table of nine concord rules with examples, covering and, each and every, as well as, either or, collective nouns, a number of, amounts, and nouns like physics and news.

sections.heading: 6. Reported speech
sections.body_md:
**Order of work:** sentence type → reporting verb and link → pronouns → tense backshift → time and place words → punctuation.

- **Statement:** *said / told + person + that* — *She said, "I am ready." → She said that she was ready.*
- **Yes/no question:** *asked + if / whether*, statement order — *"Is the shop open?" → He asked if the shop was open.*
- **Wh-question:** *asked + wh-word*, statement order — *"Why are you late?" → She asked why I was late.*
- **Command / request:** *told / ordered / advised / requested + person + (not) to + verb* — *"Please wait." → She requested me to wait.*

**No backshift** when the reporting verb is present (*says*) or for universal truths (*The teacher said that light travels faster than sound*).

key_terms.definition_md: The verb that introduces the report: said, told, asked, replied, requested, ordered, advised, enquired.

visuals.alt: Table of tense backshift in reported speech: am, is, are become was or were; do becomes did; is doing becomes was doing; did and has done become had done; will, can, may become would, could, might; must stays or becomes had to.
visuals.caption: No backshift if the reporting verb is present (says) or the statement is a universal truth.

rows: the previous day / the day before
the next day / the following day

visuals.alt: Table of time and place word changes: now to then, today to that day, yesterday to the previous day, tomorrow to the next day, ago to before, last week to the previous week, this to that, here to there.

rows: She said that she was ready.
He asked if I was ready.

visuals.alt: Table of four sentence types in reported speech: statements use said or told with that; yes or no questions use asked with if or whether; wh-questions use asked with the wh-word; commands and requests use told or requested with a to-infinitive.

sections.heading: 7. Editing and omission
sections.body_md:
**Editing:** each line or sentence has one error. Test it against the six families — tense, concord, article, preposition, pronoun, word form / spelling — and write the incorrect word with its correction.

**Omission:** one word is missing. It is usually an article, preposition, helping verb, pronoun or conjunction. Read in pairs of words, find the jolt, and write *word before + missing word + word after*.

**Frequent errors:** *discuss about, reached to, return back* (extra preposition); *a advice, an university* (articles); *did not went, has came* (verb forms); *principle / principal, their / there, its / it's* (look-alike words).

key_terms.definition_md: A word left out of a sentence; the task is to find where and supply it.

rows: He spoke confident. I will recieve it.

visuals.alt: Table of six error families in editing tasks with a wrong and a corrected example: tense, concord, article, preposition, pronoun, and word form or spelling.

nodes.label: Read the line in pairs of words
Ask: article? preposition? helper verb? pronoun?
Write word before + missing word + word after

visuals.alt: Flow of four steps for omission: read in pairs of words, find where it jolts, ask which kind of word is missing, write the words before and after with the missing word.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Marks:** 10 marks — 12 one-mark tasks, attempt any 10 (Section B, CBSE 2026-27). Some items have options; others ask you to write the word or sentence.

**How marks are awarded:** one mark for a fully correct answer. In editing, the incorrect word and the correction must both be right; in reported speech, the reporting verb, pronoun, tense and time-word changes must all be right. A misspelt answer can lose the mark.

**Common mistakes**
1. *has / have* with *yesterday, ago, last week*.
2. *did not went* — after *did*, use the base verb.
3. *must to go* — no *to* after a modal.
4. *an university, a hour* — choose by sound.
5. Concord with the nearest noun instead of the real subject (*The list of names are…*).
6. Question order in reported questions (*asked where was I going*).
7. Forgetting time words: *tomorrow → the next day*.

**Presentation:** write the item number and the answer only; in editing and omission, use the exact format the question gives.

questions.stem_md:
Choose the correct determiner.

Our class monitor is ___ honest boy who never hides a mistake.
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** an. "Honest" begins with a vowel **sound** (the *h* is silent: "on-est"), so it takes **an**. "Some" and "many" need a plural or uncountable noun, not "boy".

questions.stem_md:
Choose the correct option.

There is ___ milk left in the fridge, enough for Dadi's evening tea.
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a little. "Milk" is **uncountable**, so only *little / a little* can go with it; "a few", "few" and "many" are for countable plurals. "Enough for Dadi's tea" gives the positive sense of *a small but sufficient amount*, which is **a little**.

questions.stem_md:
Choose the correct option.

Only ___ students turned up for the 6 a.m. practice, so the coach cancelled it.
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a few. "Students" is a **countable plural**, which rules out *a little, much* and *little* (all for uncountable nouns). "Only a few" is the natural fixed pairing for a small number.

questions.stem_md: Which sentence uses the determiner correctly?

options.text_md: Every students must carry an ID card.
Each student must carry an ID card.
Each of student must carry an ID card.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Each student must carry an ID card. *Each* and *every* take a **singular** noun ("each student", "every student"). "Much" is for uncountable nouns. "Each of" needs a plural noun with a determiner ("each of the students").

questions.stem_md:
Fill in the blanks with suitable articles.

My cousin is studying to become ___ engineer, and she hopes to work for ___ Indian Space Research Organisation one day.
questions.solution_md: (1) "engineer" begins with a vowel sound → **an**. (2) A particular, unique organisation whose name contains a common noun ("Organisation") takes **the**.

questions.stem_md:
Complete the sentence with the correct word from the brackets.

There isn't ___ (much / many) sugar in the jar, so please buy a kilo.
questions.solution_md: "Sugar" is uncountable, and *much* goes with uncountable nouns, especially in negatives. *Many* is for countable plurals (many biscuits). Answer: **much**.

questions.stem_md:
Complete the sentence with the correct word from the brackets.

The shopkeeper showed me two school bags, but neither ___ (bag / bags) had a bottle pocket.
questions.solution_md: *Neither* (like *either, each, every*) is followed by a **singular** noun: "neither bag". The plural is used only with "neither of the bags". Answer: **bag**.

questions.stem_md:
Identify the error in the sentence and supply the correction.

Before the interview, my mentor gave me a useful advice.
questions.solution_md: "Advice" is an **uncountable** noun, so it cannot take *a/an*. Drop the article, or use a quantity phrase such as *some* or *a piece of*.

answer.model_answer_md: Error: **a useful advice** → Correction: **useful advice** (also accepted: *some useful advice* / *a piece of useful advice*).

questions.stem_md: Match each determiner with the meaning it gives.

match_right.text_md: some (countable) — enough to make a difference
some (uncountable) — a small but useful amount

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). With the article (*a few, a little*) the meaning is **positive**; without it (*few, little*) the meaning is **negative**. *Few* forms go with countable nouns, *little* forms with uncountable nouns.

questions.stem_md: True or false: we write "an university" because "university" begins with a vowel letter.
questions.solution_md: **False.** The choice depends on the first **sound**, not the letter. "University" begins with a "yoo" (consonant) sound, so it is **a university** — just like *a uniform* and *a European city*.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the word groups to make a correct sentence.
questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (d) → (c) → (a). The sentence is **"Each of the players has finished the warm-up drill."** *Each of* needs a plural noun phrase after it ("the players"), and the verb agrees with *each*, so it is singular: **has finished**.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md:
Fill in the blanks with suitable determiners and give a reason for each choice.

"I have (a) ___ friends in Chennai, but during exams I hardly get (b) ___ time to call them."
questions.solution_md: Step 1: decide whether each noun is countable (friends) or uncountable (time). Step 2: check the sense — "hardly" is negative, so *any/much* fit (b). *A few, some* or *many* all fit (a).

answer.model_answer_md: (a) **a few / some / many** — "friends" is a countable plural noun. (b) **any / much** — "time" here is uncountable, and "hardly" makes the sentence negative, which suits *any* or *much*.

marking_scheme.step: (b) suitable determiner with reason (uncountable, negative sense)

questions.stem_md:
Choose the correct option.

By the time the ambulance arrived, the neighbours ___ the injured cyclist into the shade.
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** had moved. Two past actions: the neighbours moved the cyclist **before** the ambulance arrived. "By the time + simple past" signals the **past perfect** for the earlier action: *had moved*.

questions.stem_md:
Choose the correct option.

Look at those dark clouds over the hills! It ___ any minute now.
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** is going to rain. We predict a future event from **present evidence** (dark clouds) with *be going to*. The simple present, simple past and present perfect do not express this prediction.

questions.stem_md:
Choose the correct option.

Ananya ___ the violin since she was seven, and she still practises every evening.
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** has been learning. *Since + a point in the past*, with the activity continuing now ("still practises"), needs the **present perfect continuous**: *has been learning*.

questions.stem_md: Which sentence shows an action that was completed **before** another past action?

options.text_md: I was eating when Papa came home.
I had already eaten when Papa came home.
I eat when Papa comes home.
I will eat when Papa comes home.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** I had already eaten when Papa came home. The past perfect *had eaten* marks the earlier of two past actions. "Was eating" shows an action in progress at the same time; the other two are present or future.

questions.stem_md:
Fill in the blanks with the correct form of the verbs in brackets.

Every morning my grandfather ___ (walk) to the temple and ___ (feed) the pigeons on the way back.
questions.solution_md: "Every morning" shows a **habit**, so use the simple present. The subject "my grandfather" is third person singular, so add -s: **walks**, **feeds**.

questions.stem_md:
Fill in the blanks with the correct form of the verbs in brackets.

While we ___ (watch) the match last night, the power ___ (go) off.
questions.solution_md: A longer action in progress (**past continuous**: *were watching*) is interrupted by a short completed action (**simple past**: *went*). The simple past *watched* is also grammatical, but *were watching* shows the interrupted action best. "Last night" fixes the time in the past.

questions.stem_md:
Fill in the blank with the correct form of the verb in brackets.

I ___ (not finish) my science project yet; I will submit it tomorrow.
questions.solution_md: "Yet" in a negative sentence about an unfinished task that matters now signals the **present perfect**: *have not finished* (or *haven't finished*).

questions.stem_md:
Fill in the blank with a correct form of the verb in brackets.

The Shatabdi ___ (leave) at 6:15 tomorrow morning, so set your alarm for five.
questions.solution_md: A timetabled future event is usually in the **simple present**: *leaves*. *Is leaving* (a fixed arrangement) and *will leave* are also correct. The time clue "tomorrow" rules out past forms.

questions.stem_md:
Fill in the blank with the correct form of the verb in brackets.

If it ___ (rain) tomorrow, the inter-house match will be postponed.
questions.solution_md: In an *if*-clause about a real future possibility, English uses the **simple present**, not *will*: "If it **rains** tomorrow, … will be postponed."

questions.stem_md:
Identify the error in the sentence and supply the correction.

We have visited the Science City in Kolkata last Sunday.
questions.solution_md: "Last Sunday" is a finished, definite past time. The present perfect cannot be used with such time expressions, so the simple past *visited* is needed.

answer.model_answer_md: Error: **have visited** → Correction: **visited**.

questions.stem_md:
Identify the error in the sentence and supply the correction.

Kabir did not went to his coaching class yesterday.
questions.solution_md: After the auxiliary *did / did not*, the main verb is always in the **base form**: "did not **go**". The past tense is already carried by *did*.

answer.model_answer_md: Error: **went** → Correction: **go**.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The sentence "She has gone to Shimla last week" is incorrect.

**Reason (R):** The present perfect is not used with an expression of definite past time such as "last week".

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The sentence is wrong (it should be "She **went** to Shimla last week"), and the reason given is exactly the rule that makes it wrong. Both are true, and R explains A.

questions.stem_md: True or false: in "The Earth goes round the Sun", the simple present is used because the sentence states a universal truth.
questions.solution_md: **True.** Facts that are always true (scientific facts, general truths) are written in the **simple present**.

questions.stem_md:
Each sentence has one tense error. Rewrite the sentences correctly.

(a) I am knowing the answer to this riddle.
(b) When I reached the station, the train already left.
questions.solution_md: (a) *Know* is a **state verb**, which is not normally used in the continuous form, so "am knowing" becomes *know*. (b) The train left **before** I reached, so the earlier past action takes the past perfect: *had already left*.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) I **know** the answer to this riddle.

(b) When I reached the station, the train **had already left**.

questions.stem_md:
Choose the correct modal.

You ___ wear a helmet when you ride a scooter; it is the law.
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** must. "It is the law" shows a **compulsory obligation**, which is expressed by *must*. *Might/could* show possibility; *need not* says it is not necessary.

questions.stem_md:
Choose the correct modal.

___ I borrow your geometry box for the test, please?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** May. Asking for **permission** politely uses *may* (or *can/could*). *Must* and *should* express obligation and advice, and *ought* needs *to* and is not used to ask permission.

questions.stem_md:
Choose the correct option.

You ___ come to school tomorrow; it is a holiday for Guru Nanak Jayanti.
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** need not. A holiday makes coming **unnecessary**, not forbidden. *Need not* = it is not necessary. *Must not* would mean you are not allowed to come; *should/must* would mean you ought to or have to come.

questions.stem_md: Which sentence makes a **polite request**?

options.text_md: You need not lower the volume.
Could you please lower the volume?

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Could you please lower the volume? *Could you … ?* with *please* is the polite request form. *Must* is an order, *might* suggests a possibility, and *need not* removes the obligation.

questions.stem_md:
Fill in the blank with the correct form of the modal in brackets.

When she was only five, my sister ___ (can) name all the state capitals.
questions.solution_md: Ability in the **past** ("when she was only five") uses *could*, the past form of *can*.

questions.stem_md:
Complete the sentence with the correct option from the brackets.

You look exhausted after the long bus ride. You ___ (should / must not) lie down for a while.
questions.solution_md: The speaker is giving **advice**, which is expressed by *should*. *Must not* is a prohibition and does not fit the caring meaning.

questions.stem_md:
Identify the error in the sentence and supply the correction.

All applicants must to submit the form before Friday.
questions.solution_md: Modals such as *must, can, should, may* are followed directly by the **base form** of the verb, without *to*. (*Ought to* and *have to* are the exceptions.)

answer.model_answer_md: Error: **must to submit** → Correction: **must submit**.

questions.stem_md: Match each modal with the function it usually expresses.
questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). *Can* — ability (I can swim); *must* — obligation (You must sign here); *should* — advice (You should rest); *might* — a weak possibility (It might drizzle).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** "You must not use your phone in the exam hall" expresses a prohibition.

**Reason (R):** "Must not" means that something is not necessary.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: *must not* forbids an action. R is false: "not necessary" is the meaning of *need not* / *don't have to*, not *must not*.

questions.stem_md: True or false: "You need not bring a lunch box" and "You must not bring a lunch box" mean the same thing.
questions.solution_md: **False.** The first says bringing one is **unnecessary** (you may if you like); the second **forbids** it.

questions.stem_md:
Rewrite each sentence using a suitable modal so that it expresses the meaning given in brackets.

(a) It is possible that the results will come out today. (possibility)
(b) It is not necessary for you to bring a gift to the party. (absence of necessity)
questions.solution_md: (a) Possibility → *may* or *might* + base verb. (b) Absence of necessity → *need not* (or *don't have to*) + base verb. *Must not* would change the meaning to a prohibition.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The results **may / might** come out today.

(b) You **need not** bring a gift to the party.

marking_scheme.step: (b) need not / don't have to + bring

questions.stem_md:
Choose the correct option.

The list of selected candidates ___ been put up on the notice board.
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** has. The real subject is **"the list"** (singular); "of selected candidates" only describes it. So the verb is singular: *has been put up*.

questions.stem_md:
Choose the correct option.

Neither the coach nor the players ___ happy with the umpire's decision.
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** were. With *neither … nor*, the verb agrees with the **nearer** subject. "The players" is plural, and the sentence is about a past decision, so *were*.

questions.stem_md:
Choose the correct option.

The school cricket team ___ its kit for the tournament in Mysuru.
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** has packed. The pronoun **its** shows the team is being treated as **one unit**, so the verb must be singular: *has packed*. The plural forms clash with "its".

questions.stem_md:
Choose the correct option.

A number of students ___ volunteered for the cleanliness drive.
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** have. *A number of* means "many", so it takes a **plural** verb: *have volunteered*. (Compare: *The number of* volunteers **is** rising.)

questions.stem_md:
Fill in the blanks with the correct option from the brackets.

Mathematics ___ (is / are) my favourite subject, but the news about the exam dates ___ (has / have) worried me.
questions.solution_md: *Mathematics* and *news* end in -s but are **singular** nouns, so they take *is* and *has*.

questions.stem_md:
Fill in the blank with the correct option from the brackets.

Each of the girls in the choir ___ (has / have) a solo line in the Independence Day song.
questions.solution_md: The subject is **each** (singular), not "girls". *Each of + plural noun* takes a singular verb: **has**.

questions.stem_md:
Identify the error in the sentence and supply the correction.

The principal, along with the teachers, are attending the seminar in Bhopal.
questions.solution_md: Phrases like *along with, as well as, together with* do not add to the subject. The subject is "the principal" (singular), so the verb is **is attending**.

answer.model_answer_md: Error: **are** → Correction: **is**.

questions.stem_md:
Identify the error in the sentence and supply the correction.

Five hundred rupees are too much to spend on a one-day school trip.
questions.solution_md: An amount of money, time or distance thought of as **one total** takes a singular verb: "Five hundred rupees **is** too much."

answer.model_answer_md: Error: **are** → Correction: **is**.

questions.stem_md: True or false: in "Idli and sambar is my usual breakfast", the singular verb is correct because the two nouns name one dish.
questions.solution_md: **True.** When two nouns joined by *and* name **one thing or one idea** (a single dish here), the verb is singular.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** "Either my parents or my uncle is coming to the parent-teacher meeting" is correct.

**Reason (R):** With *either … or*, the verb agrees with the subject that is nearer to it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The nearer subject is "my uncle" (singular), so *is coming* is correct. The rule in R is exactly why A is correct.

questions.stem_md:
The sentence below has two errors. Rewrite it correctly.

"Each of the boys have brought there own lunch."
questions.solution_md: (1) Concord: the subject is *each* (singular) → **has**. (2) Spelling of the possessive: *there* (a place) → **their** (belonging to them). (*His own lunch* is also accepted for the pronoun.)

answer.model_answer_md: Each of the boys **has** brought **their** own lunch.

questions.stem_md:
Choose the correct reported form.

Rohan said, "I am tired after the drill."

options.text_md: Rohan said that I was tired after the drill.
Rohan said that he was tired after the drill.
Rohan told that he was tired after the drill.
Rohan said that he has been tired after the drill.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Rohan said that he was tired after the drill. Change **I → he** (Rohan is speaking about himself) and backshift **am → was** after the past reporting verb *said*. *Told* needs an object (told **me / us**), so "told that" is wrong.

questions.stem_md:
Choose the correct reported form.

The teacher said to us, "Do not run in the corridor."

options.text_md: The teacher told us that do not run in the corridor.
The teacher said us not to run in the corridor.
The teacher told us don't run in the corridor.
The teacher told us not to run in the corridor.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The teacher told us not to run in the corridor. A negative **command** becomes *told / ordered / warned* + object + **not to** + base verb. "Said us" is ungrammatical (*said to us*), and a command is not reported with *that*.

questions.stem_md:
Choose the correct reported form.

Meena asked me, "Where do you live?"

options.text_md: Meena asked me where I lived.
Meena asked me where did I live.
Meena asked me where do I live.
Meena asked me that where I lived.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Meena asked me where I lived. A *wh*-question keeps the *wh*-word as the link, changes to **statement order** (subject before verb: *I lived*), drops *do/did*, and loses the question mark. *That* is never added before the *wh*-word.

questions.stem_md:
Report the following question.

Papa said to me, "Have you fed the dog?"
questions.solution_md: A yes/no question is reported with **asked + if/whether**. *You → I*, present perfect *have fed* → past perfect **had fed**, statement order, no question mark.

answer.model_answer_md: Papa asked me **if / whether I had fed** the dog.

marking_scheme.step: Suitable reporting verb and linking word (that / if / whether / wh-word / to)
Pronoun, tense and time-word changes all correct

questions.stem_md:
Report the following request.

The conductor said to the passengers, "Please move to the back of the bus."
questions.solution_md: A request uses *requested / asked* + object + **to-infinitive**. *Please* is dropped because the reporting verb *requested* already carries the politeness.

answer.model_answer_md: The conductor **requested / asked** the passengers **to move** to the back of the bus.

marking_scheme.step: Reporting verb requested / asked with the object
to move … (to-infinitive, rest of sentence correct)

questions.stem_md:
Report the following statement.

Priya said to me, "I will call you tomorrow."
questions.solution_md: *Said to me* → **told me**; *I → she*, *you → me*; *will → would*; *tomorrow* → **the next day / the following day** (the time reference shifts because the report is made later).

answer.model_answer_md: Priya **told me that she would call me the next day** (or *the following day*).

marking_scheme.step: Suitable reporting verb and linking word (that / if / whether / wh-word / to)
Pronoun, tense and time-word changes all correct

questions.stem_md:
Complete the reported version.

Asha said to her friend, "I bought this kurta yesterday."

Asha told her friend that she ___ that kurta ___.
questions.solution_md: Simple past *bought* → past perfect **had bought**; *this → that*; *yesterday* → **the previous day** (or *the day before*).

marking_scheme.step: Blank 2: the previous day / the day before

questions.stem_md: Arrange the word groups to make the correct reported question.
questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (e) → (a) → (d) → (c) → (b). The reported question is **"The librarian asked me whether I had returned the encyclopaedia."** Reporting verb + object, then *whether*, then **statement order** (*I had returned*).

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Match each word in direct speech with its usual change in reported speech (when the report is made later, somewhere else).
questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(q), (d)–(s). Time and place words shift because the report is made at a different time and place: *now → then, yesterday → the previous day, tomorrow → the next day, here → there*.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** "Our physics teacher said that water boils at 100 °C at sea level" correctly reports a universal fact.

**Reason (R):** The reporting verb "said" is in the past tense.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is true: a universal truth keeps the present tense even after a past reporting verb. R is also true, but it does not explain A — normally a past reporting verb causes a backshift, so R is not the reason the present tense is kept.

questions.stem_md: True or false: commands are usually reported with a *to*-infinitive after verbs such as *ordered*, *told* or *advised*.
questions.solution_md: **True.** E.g. "Sit down," the umpire said to him → The umpire **told him to sit** down.

questions.stem_md:
Report the dialogue.

Coach: "Why are you late again?"

Arjun: "My bus broke down near the flyover."
questions.solution_md: Line 1 is a *wh*-question: *asked* + *why* + statement order, *you → he*, *are → was*. Line 2 is a statement: *replied that*, *my → his*, *broke down → had broken down* (backshift of the simple past).

answer.model_answer_md: The coach asked Arjun **why he was late again**. Arjun replied that **his bus had broken down** near the flyover.

marking_scheme.step: Question reported correctly (asked + why + he was, statement order)
Reply reported correctly (replied that + his bus had broken down)

questions.stem_md:
Report the dialogue.

Grandmother: "Switch off the fan before you leave the room."

Vivek: "I always do that, Dadi."
questions.solution_md: Line 1 is a command: *told/reminded* + object + **to-infinitive**, *you leave → he left*. Line 2 is a statement: *replied that*, *I → he*, *do → did*. The form of address *Dadi* is dropped and its respect is shown by *respectfully*.

answer.model_answer_md: Vivek's grandmother **told / reminded him to switch off** the fan before he left the room. Vivek **respectfully replied that he always did that**.

marking_scheme.step: Command reported (told/reminded him to switch off; he left)
Statement reported (replied that he always did that)

questions.stem_md:
Read the conversation at a stationery shop and report it in a paragraph.

Nidhi: "Do you have the new graph notebooks?"

Shopkeeper: "They will arrive on Monday."

Nidhi: "Can you keep two for me?"

Shopkeeper: "Of course. Please pay an advance of fifty rupees."

Nidhi: "Thank you. I will come back on Monday."
questions.solution_md: Report each line by its type: yes/no question → *asked whether/if*; statement → *replied that* with *will → would*; question with *can* → *asked if he could*; "Of course" → *readily agreed*; request → *requested her to pay*; "Thank you" → *thanked him*; final statement → *said that she would*. "On Monday" may stay because the day is named, not relative.

answer.model_answer_md: Nidhi asked the shopkeeper **whether he had** the new graph notebooks. The shopkeeper replied that **they would arrive** on Monday. Nidhi then asked him **if he could keep** two for her. The shopkeeper readily agreed and **requested her to pay** an advance of fifty rupees. Nidhi thanked him and said that **she would come back** on Monday.

marking_scheme.step: Line 3: question with can (if he could keep)
Line 4: agreement + request (requested her to pay)
Line 5: thanks + statement (she would come back); paragraph reads smoothly

questions.stem_md:
Identify the error in the sentence and supply the correction.

The students was asked to assemble in the playground after lunch.
questions.solution_md: The subject "the students" is plural, so the passive auxiliary must be plural: *were asked*.

answer.model_answer_md: Error: **was** → Correction: **were**.

questions.stem_md:
One word is missing in the sentence. Write the missing word along with the words that come before and after it.

My younger brother is very fond playing chess with our grandfather.
questions.solution_md: The adjective *fond* is always followed by the preposition **of**: "fond of playing". Write the words on both sides so the examiner sees the exact place.

answer.model_answer_md: fond **of** playing

marking_scheme.step: Place of the omission identified (words before and after)

questions.stem_md:
One word is missing in the sentence. Write the missing word along with the words that come before and after it.

Shreya is best singer in our school choir.
questions.solution_md: A **superlative** adjective (*best, tallest, most useful*) needs *the* before it: "is the best singer".

answer.model_answer_md: is **the** best

marking_scheme.step: Place of the omission identified (words before and after)

questions.stem_md:
Identify the error in the sentence and supply the correction.

We discussed about the new timetable in the class meeting.
questions.solution_md: *Discuss* is a transitive verb: it takes a direct object without *about* ("discussed the timetable"). (*A discussion about* is fine, because *discussion* is a noun.)

answer.model_answer_md: Error: **discussed about** → Correction: **discussed** (no preposition).

questions.stem_md:
Identify the error in the sentence and supply the correction.

The principle announced the board results in the morning assembly.
questions.solution_md: *Principal* = the head of a school; *principle* = a rule or belief. The person who announced the results is the **principal**.

answer.model_answer_md: Error: **principle** → Correction: **principal**.

questions.stem_md:
Choose the option that corrects the error in the sentence.

"Neither of the answers are correct."

options.text_md: Neither of the answer are correct.
Neither of the answers were correct.
Neither of the answers is correct.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Neither of the answers is correct. *Neither of + plural noun* takes a **singular** verb in formal English (the subject is *neither* = not one). The noun after *of the* stays plural.

questions.stem_md:
Fill in the blank with a suitable preposition.

My classmate Farhan has been absent ___ Monday because of viral fever.
questions.solution_md: With the present perfect continuous, a **point** in time (Monday) takes *since*; a **period** (three days) takes *for*. Answer: **since**.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An omission task tests only spelling.

**Reason (R):** An omission task asks you to find the place where a word has been left out and to supply that word.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: the missing word may be an article, preposition, auxiliary, pronoun or conjunction — it tests grammar, not spelling. R correctly describes the task.

questions.stem_md:
The notice below has two errors. Rewrite the notice sentence correctly.

"All the student of Class X are informed that a extra class will be held on Saturday."
questions.solution_md: (1) *All the* + plural noun, and the plural verb *are* → **students**. (2) *Extra* begins with a vowel sound → **an** extra class.

answer.model_answer_md: All the **students** of Class X are informed that **an** extra class will be held on Saturday.

questions.stem_md:
Each sentence of the paragraph below has one error. Rewrite the paragraph correctly and underline the corrected words.

"Last month our school organise a book fair. More than forty publishers sets up stalls in the hall. Every visitors received a free bookmark. I buyed two novels and an atlas. My friends and I has decided to start a reading club."
questions.solution_md: 1. "Last month" → simple past *organised*. 2. Plural subject "publishers" and past time → *set* (past of *set* is *set*). 3. *Every* + singular noun → *visitor*. 4. The past of *buy* is irregular → *bought*. 5. The compound subject "My friends and I" is plural → *have decided*.

answer.model_answer_md: Last month our school **organised** a book fair. More than forty publishers **set** up stalls in the hall. Every **visitor** received a free bookmark. I **bought** two novels and an atlas. My friends and I **have** decided to start a reading club.

questions.stem_md: The passage below has **one error in each numbered line**. For each line, identify the incorrect word and supply the correction.
questions.solution_md: Read each line on its own. Find the subject and the time frame first; most errors are concord (lines 1, 5), tense (lines 3, 4) or a noun after a number (line 2).

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** celebrates; celebrate

**(b)** hour; hours

**(c)** sings; sang

**(d)** shout; shouted

**(e)** make; makes

questions.passage_md:
(1) Every year the residents of our building celebrates Pongal together in the courtyard.

(2) This year the children decorated the entrance with a kolam that took them three hour to finish.

(3) The elders cooked sweet pongal in a large brass pot while we sings folk songs.

(4) When the milk boiled over, everyone shout "Pongalo Pongal!" in joy.

(5) The festival reminds us that sharing food make neighbours feel like one family.

children.solution_md: The real subject is "the residents" (plural); "of our building" only describes them. So **celebrate** replaces *celebrates*.
*Three* needs a plural noun: **hours** replaces *hour*.
The passage is in the past ("cooked") and "we" is plural → **sang** (or *were singing*) replaces *sings*.
A completed past action triggered by "boiled over" → **shouted** replaces *shout*.
The subject of the *that*-clause is "sharing food" (a gerund phrase, singular) → **makes** replaces *make*.

questions.stem_md: Read the message a student wrote on her class WhatsApp group and choose the correct option for each numbered blank.
questions.solution_md: For each blank look at the words around it: the subject (concord), the time clue (tense), the meaning (modal) and the next noun (determiner).

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (c) is the

**(b)** (a) must

**(c)** (d) have

**(d)** (b) a

**(e)** (a) needs

questions.passage_md: Hi everyone! Tomorrow (a) ___ last day to submit the photographs for the Earth Day exhibition. Ma'am says each of us (b) ___ bring at least two prints. I (c) ___ already printed mine at the shop near the bus stop, so I can share tips today. The owner gave me (d) ___ discount because we bought in bulk. If anyone (e) ___ help with editing, message me tonight.

children.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** is the. A unique, specific day → *the last day*; the subject "tomorrow" is singular → *is*.
**Correct option: (a)** must. The teacher's instruction is an **obligation** → *must*.
**Correct option: (d)** have. *Already* + a past action with a present result → present perfect with *I*: *have printed*.
**Correct option: (b)** a. "Discount" is a countable noun here beginning with a consonant sound → *a discount*.
**Correct option: (a)** needs. *Anyone* is singular, and an *if*-clause about the future uses the simple present → *needs*.

questions.stem_md: In each numbered line of the passage, **one word has been omitted**. Supply the missing word.
questions.solution_md: Read each line in pairs of words and listen for the gap: articles before singular countable nouns, auxiliaries before past participles, prepositions after verbs.
questions.passage_md:
(1) Last Saturday our NCC unit went on trek to a fort near Lonavala.

(2) We started at dawn because the climb takes about three hours in monsoon.

(3) Halfway up, one the cadets slipped and hurt her ankle.

(4) Our officer, who is trained in first aid, bandaged quickly.

(5) We reached top just as the clouds opened up below us.

children.solution_md: "Trek" is a singular countable noun → *on **a** trek*.

children.stem_md: Line (2): about three hours in ___ monsoon
children.solution_md: We say *in **the** monsoon* (the season).
One member of a group is *one **of** the cadets*; the preposition *of* links *one* to the group.
*Bandage* is transitive and needs an object; the ankle is referred to by the pronoun **it**: *bandaged **it** quickly*.
A specific top (of that fort) → *reached **the** top*.

questions.stem_md: Read the conversation between a student and the school librarian, then complete the reported version.
questions.solution_md: Identify the sentence type first (yes/no question, statement, command, request), then choose the reporting verb and link word, then make the pronoun, tense and time changes.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** if

**(b)** might; to return

**(c)** was

**(d)** had borrowed

**(e)** requested

questions.passage_md:
Kavya: "Can I borrow two books this week?"

Librarian: "You may take two, but return them by Friday."

Kavya: "Is the new atlas available?"

Librarian: "Someone borrowed it yesterday."

Kavya: "Please keep it for me when it comes back."

children.stem_md: Kavya asked the librarian ___ she could borrow two books that week.
children.solution_md: A yes/no question is reported with **if** or **whether**.

children.stem_md: The librarian replied that she ___ take two, but told her ___ them by Friday.
children.solution_md: *May* (permission) backshifts to **might** (or *could*); the command "return them" becomes **to return**.

children.stem_md: Kavya then asked whether the new atlas ___ available.
children.solution_md: Backshift of *is* → **was**, in statement order after *whether*.

children.stem_md: The librarian said that someone ___ it the previous day.
children.solution_md: Simple past *borrowed* → past perfect **had borrowed**; *yesterday → the previous day*.

children.stem_md: Kavya ___ the librarian to keep it for her when it came back.
children.solution_md: A request with *please* is reported with **requested** (or *asked*) + object + *to*-infinitive.
